To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the descending pathways that regulate hind limb muscle blood flow originate in the RVLM and include catecholaminergie neurons.

the RVLM is the primary site of origin of the descending pathways that regulate muscle blood pressure and that the RVLM has the capacity to independently regulate the blood pressure in the left and the right hindlimb.

the descending neural pathways that control muscle blood flow are bilateral, involve catecholaminergics in the RVLM, and have a limited capacity to regulate left and right hind limb muscle blood flow independently.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural control of muscle blood flow and the role of the brain in the regulation of blood flow.
the neural mechanisms that underlie the regulation of blood flow to the hindlimb muscles of the rat.
the neural mechanisms regulating muscle blood flow.

the descending pathways that regulate muscle bloodflow are complex and that the RVLM is a major, but not exclusive, component of these pathways.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

PRV-152 is a useful tool for mapping the neural pathways that control sympathetic nerve activity to skeletal muscles, and that the RVLM, in addition to the medullary raphespinal neurons, is an important brain stem area for regulating muscle blood flow.

the RVLM and the raphe nuclei are the primary brain stem sites from which the sympathetic nerves to hindlimb muscles are regulated, and that there are few, if any, descending pathways that are specific for the regulation of muscle blood flow.

PRV tracing of the neural pathways controlling hindlimb muscle sympathetic outflow revealed that the RVLM plays the dominant role, and that the RVLM is reciprocally connected to the medullary nuclei of the raphe, locus coeruleal complex, and paraventricular hypothalamus.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the brain stem areas that regulate muscle bloodflow appear to be interconnected, and this interconnection is likely to be important for integrating the sympathetic outflow that regulates muscle blood flow.
the RVLM, a brain stem region that has been implicated in a number of other functions, is a key regulator of muscle blood flow.

the RVLM, the medullary serotonergic cell groups, and the hypothalamic paraventricular and dorsomedial nuclei are the brain stem regions that play the largest role, and the locus coeruleus and the A5 region play the smallest roles, in the central regulation of hindlimb muscle sympathetic nerve activity and blood flow.
